# 08-fresco — sources

Back-test entry `08-fresco.yaml`: Fresco, the AI scribe for construction superintendents (YC Fall 2024).
Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim from the page named; "Author's choice" marks the
smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent.

Main sources:
- [HN] Launch HN: Fresco (YC F24), 2024-11-21 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42204939
- [LYC] Launch YC: Fresco, the scribe for construction, 2024-10-23 — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/M73-fresco-the-scribe-for-construction
- [YCP] YC company page — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/fresco (now "AI-powered takeoff and estimating for Division 8 construction")
- [KOE] A contractor's daily-log expectations on Procore's support site — https://support.procore.com/tc/Koester/Site_Map/Koester_Expectations_-_Daily_Logs
- [SWI] Swiftask, Procore daily reports page (vendor) — https://swiftask.ai/ai-integration/procore/intelligent-daily-reports
- [BLS] BLS Occupational Outlook, construction managers — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/management/construction-managers.htm
- [OPU] Launch HN: Opusense (field reports for site inspectors), 2025-05-20 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44042791

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Construction superintendents on commercial jobs.
   [HN] "Superintendents are the busiest and most expensive people on construction sites."
   [LYC] "That’s the reality for 210k+ construction superintendents (or supervisors, foremen, PMs, etc.) across the USA."
   → `roles[superintendent]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: "on commercial jobs" (the founders ask
   for introductions to commercial general contractors in [LYC]).

2. **What (the job).** Keep the record of the day's work, for liability and disputes.
   [HN] "30-200 photos per day to document site progress (mostly for liability reasons, or in case of a dispute with the
   owner over delays and deliverables)"; photos used to create "daily logs", "structured documents that account for the
   work done on site on any given day". [KOE] the log is "a critical piece of documentation in the arbitration of a
   dispute". → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At the end of the day, after the site walks, in the trailer.
   [HN] "At the end of the day, they'll spend a few hours uploading those photos into OneDrive, or project management
   software like Procore or ACC." [YCP] "We were curious what superintendents were doing for hours in their trailers at
   the end of the day." [LYC] "supes are spending up to 3 hours a day creating documents". → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: daily log`.
   Author's choice: the recall window {5, WORKING_DAYS} and Frequency 4 to 5 working days out of 5 (the posts say "per
   day"; a five-day site week is assumed). Prevalence `p_80_100` ("Nearly all") follows from the same "per day".

4. **Which people (the comparable group).** Superintendents at US general contractors whose jobs run on Procore or ACC.
   [LYC] "210k+ construction superintendents ... across the USA"; "Project management tools like Procore and ACC have
   dramatically increased documentation requirements". [YCP] "driving to Napa, South Bay, and around SF". → `context.segment`,
   `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The general contractor, per site.
   [HN] "we charge per site per month, which includes unlimited users on any given construction project".
   → `persona.decision_maker: {role: contractor}`, the BUYER role. Author's choice: the decider is the contractor's
   "operations lead" and the role to test is "The CFO" (a second role, "The project executive", listed); Purchase
   friction's three steps ("A trial on one live job" tested, a Procore check, a security review) and Commitment's step
   "start a paid pilot on one site" are the author's. Public material names no buyer title; [LYC] asks for
   introductions to general contractors by firm, not by role.

6. **Mechanism.** Narrated short videos turned into notes, texted to the crew, pushed to Procore/ACC.
   [HN] "Supers simply take short videos with voiceover, or upload photos, and Fresco does the rest, creating notes with
   transcription, photos, assignees, and due dates. Supers can easily text their crew action items, and receive texts
   back". "We also route this to whatever project management software they're using with a single click."
   [LYC] the narrated example "The beam in the southwest corner of room 134 is corroded and needs replacement by Alex.";
   "Supes who use Fresco complete their notes, on average, 90% faster."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility and Adoption friction items. Relative advantage's two
   benefits are from [HN] ("during their site walks, not after") and [LYC] ("90% faster"); their wording is the author's.

7. **Price.** About $1k per site per month, less with multi-site or multi-month terms.
   [HN] "The typical price is $1k/month, but we offer discounts for multi-month or multi-site commitments."
   → `commercial.price` {800, 1000, month}. Author's choice: the low end of $800 stands for the stated discounts.
   Existing sacrifice: 30 to 60 hours a month per site at an hourly rate of 55 — from [LYC] "up to 3 hours a day" and
   [HN] "a few hours uploading", taken as 1.5 to 3 hours on about twenty working days (author's arithmetic). The rate is
   [BLS] "$55.28 per hour" (median, construction managers, May 2025), the author's stand-in: no superintendent wage is
   in the public material. Ability to pay is derived by code (24% to 61%).

8. **Occasions.** The narrated beam; a school refit report; the uploads and logs at the end of the day.
   [LYC] on a school refit walkthrough: "Normally, creating the final report takes 2+ hours."
   [HN] "few supers have time to do this thoroughly, so these photos aren't very searchable." No named customer quote
   exists in public; the occasions below are scripted from these and from practitioner comments.

## Open
- The verdict was scripted to be plausible and not obviously "build": the problem holds on how often but people
  disagree on whether the log is one of their two worst difficulties; the solution splits on the benefit and on
  talking over videos on site; the price fails (two of eight at the founder's band or above) while the cost it would
  replace is above the price. This is the author's reading of the thread's sceptics, not a measured result.
- No public account names a buyer title at a general contractor; the decider, the tested role "The CFO", the purchase
  steps and the Commitment step are the author's.
- hourly_rate 55 is a proxy (construction managers, not superintendents).
- Existing sacrifice picks use `period: quarter` (the corpus's convention), although the registry's recall period for a
  monthly cost reads "last month"; the values are the monthly figures times three.
- The window {5, WORKING_DAYS} is the author's; the public posts say "per day".

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Trevor's answer is about a known $600 monthly cost that caps the price, not about logs costing little, so it sits oddly beside Faith's, while the other placements and the plain names hold up.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line, so nothing needed keeping out.

founder.order_why: It runs the way I'd pitch Fresco: who the supers are and the end-of-day log first, then the problem, then the narrated-video scribe, then who pays (the GC, per site) and how a GC buys, and last who gets the study.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 20 and 22: screen 20 already set the first step as a paid pilot on one site, and screen 22 asks again whether to offer a pilot. Screens 3 and 4 also show the same kicker and question, so they read as one screen asked twice even if they collect different fields. Screen 2's where-you-sell overlaps the context's where: US.
founder.missing: The price's unit and terms: Fresco is charged per site per month with unlimited users, and cheaper on multi-site or multi-month terms, but screen 13 only asks for a price. Also missing: the crew and subs who get the texted action items and text back, a second set of users whose uptake matters.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: It goes from the time we spend now, to what it's worth, to who signs, to the Procore check, to whether I'd pilot, which is how I'd actually think through buying it; the follow-up just sits where question 3 would be.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: Whether the per-site price covers unlimited users (supers, PMs, foremen and subs on the log) or charges per seat, and how many active sites we run, since that decides what this costs us in total.

screens.why2: "Contractor operations lead" is my own pick for the decider, and "who has to agree before they can buy" is how anyone selling to a GC talks about getting a purchase approved.
screens.why3: I sell to general contractors, so I know a $1k-a-month line item usually needs a nod from finance and from the project exec running the job.
screens.why4: There's a free box for up to two roles, "Nobody" is allowed, and the only chip is I'm not sure, which is the founder-side escape the card asks for.
screens.why5: It keeps my decider, the contractor operations lead, word for word, and leaves my two roles for me to type.
screens.why7: The box matches the card's founder list: at most two roles besides the decider, each up to 4 words, nobody allowed, and I'm not sure as the only escape that leaves the dimension out.

screens.why1: Right after I named who has to agree besides my ops lead, it is natural to see the list Keel built from it and check it.
screens.why2: Superintendent, operations lead, CFO and project executive are the titles I use at a GC, and the tags are plain words.
screens.why3: Who uses it, who signs and who has to agree at a general contractor is what I learn on every sales call.
screens.why4: The rows are my two roles in my order, the super and ops lead tagged correctly, nothing added or dropped, with Nobody else fixed first.
screens.why5: It still says what I typed: the ops lead decides, and the CFO and the project executive have to agree.
screens.why7: Nobody else first, then at most two has-to-agree roles in my words and order, each tagged, the user and decider on separate rows as they are different people, so a belief naming both roles follows.

screens.why1: Right after I named the CFO and the project executive as the people who have to agree, and checked Keel's rows, it makes sense to pick what the test will carry: me deciding alone, or me deciding with those two signing off.
screens.why2: Two rows in words any GC ops lead or super uses daily (CFO, project executive, has to agree), and the intro says in one line what the decider will be asked.
screens.why3: Who signs off on a per-site software subscription at a general contractor is exactly what I learned selling Fresco, so I can choose from what I know.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct and complete for this choice (decides alone, or decides with the CFO and the project executive), my roles are in my titles and order, and nothing is added or dropped; only the untagged *Nobody else* sits a little unevenly next to the tagged row.
screens.why5: The belief and bar keep both roles I typed, the CFO and the project executive, behind the contractor operations lead, with nothing dropped or turned into *nobody else*.
screens.why7: The Choose screen offers the card's two tests (decider alone, or decider with every role tagged *has to agree*), the belief joins both roles with *and*, the bar counts *could sign off myself* and *the role would have to agree* as For so it can hold or fail at 2 in 3, and no escape is needed here; that the stranger's item will name only the CFO is the card's Open point, not a fault of this screen.

screens.why1: Right after who has to agree, asking what my buyer's side must clear before paying is the obvious next step in how it sells.
screens.why2: Steps, buyer's own side, security review are plain to me as a founder selling to general contractors, and the hint's example makes it clear.
screens.why3: I know what a GC checks before buying field software: Procore fit and what happens to site video.
screens.why4: It is a free-text box with one escape, I'm not sure, which fits a founder who cannot name the steps.
screens.why5: My two steps are kept in my words, with the trial already dropped as my own offer.
screens.why7: Both rows are buyer-side brakes I do not control, each under 9 words with its object, biggest first; but the Procore check partly restates my own pitch that it routes to Procore with one click, which the card says should not be a step.
screens.instead: What must the contractor clear before paying for Fresco? e.g. A security review of the site videos; IT sign-off on a new app on supers' phones

screens.why1: Right after I named what the contractor must clear, Keel shows back the list it drafted for me to check, which is exactly where this belongs.
screens.why2: The three rows are plain construction talk to me, but the line under them, 'Keel's draft broke one of its own rules,' tells me something is wrong without saying which rule or which row, so I'd read it twice and still not know what to fix.
screens.why3: A GC checking it works with Procore, IT looking at where the site videos go, and legal asking about filming crews are all things I've heard from contractors I sell to.
screens.why4: Three distinct steps, each on the GC's side with its object named, none overlapping, and Keel's one added row is a real gate I hadn't typed: recording workers on site in two-party-consent states like California, or on union jobs.
screens.why5: My Procore check and my security review of the site videos are kept in my words, the trial I'd first listed is gone as the revision says, and nothing reads as my pitch.
screens.why7: The rows are buyer-side brakes with their objects, there are 1 to 4 of them with no overlaps and no trial or pilot of mine, and Keel added one tagged row that is a real gate for this trade and place rather than a formality, so the time I type next can be tested against bands.
screens.instead: Same three rows (A check that it works with Procore or ACC · A security review of the site videos · A legal review of recording workers on site, Keel's suggestion), with the 'broke one of its own rules' line replaced by what was changed and why, or removed.

screens.why1: Right after I checked the list of what the contractor's side has to clear, it's obvious I now pick the one step to test and say how long I think it takes.
screens.why2: A Procore check, a security review of the site videos and a legal review of recording workers are all things a GC's ops people actually say, and the intro and time box read in one pass.
screens.why3: I've sat through these with GCs and know roughly how long an ops lead takes to confirm something pushes into Procore, so I can answer from my own sales.
screens.why4: Three distinct buyer-side steps with no overlap; Keel's added legal review is a real gate for filming crews in places like California, and I'm not sure fits as the escape.
screens.why5: My Procore check and the security review are in my words, my 2 weeks is what I typed, and the belief names my decider, the contractor operations lead.
screens.why7: The picked step is a brake on the buyer's side, not my own pilot or offer, the time is mine (2 weeks), and the bar matches the card. The scale is under 1 week, 1 to under 2 weeks, then from 2 weeks up, plus not needed, so the belief can hold or fail. Keel added only one row, a real gate, and the escape is the only chip.

screens.why1: After the price, the sign-offs and the purchase hurdles, the next thing I'd want to say is what I'd ask a GC's ops lead to do first, so this lands in the right place.
screens.why2: 'First real step' and 'pay for a pilot' are how I'd talk about selling to a general contractor, and the hint makes clear that both halves of the question fit in one short phrase.
screens.why3: This is my own sales motion, and I know I want a paid pilot on one live job before anything bigger.
screens.why4: The only option is the 'I'm not sure' escape, which fits a founder who hasn't settled the first step, and the box took my nine words without trouble.
screens.why5: My words, 'start a paid pilot on one site', go in as I'd say them, and the hint promises that the smaller free step is drafted next for me to keep or change rather than slipped in here.
screens.why7: The box asks for what the card wants: one step of up to nine words, in base form, said by the person who takes it, naming where the money goes, and it flags the smaller step only when the step costs money, data or a signature; the founder's 'I'm not sure' is allowed.

screens.why1: Once I've named the paid pilot as my first step, checking how strangers will hear it, and what free step comes before it, is the obvious next thing to do.
screens.why2: 'Start a paid pilot on one site' and 'a demo on sample data' are the words I use with GCs, and an ops lead reads them at a glance.
screens.why3: Whether to pilot a tool on one job is exactly the call a contractor's operations lead makes, so they can answer from their own work.
screens.why4: The four answers are a firm yes, a soft yes after a free demo, probably not and no; they are distinct, they cover the real answers, and there is correctly no escape.
screens.why5: My step is kept word for word, including 'paid' and 'one site', the decider is the contractor operations lead I named, and the free demo on sample data is a fair smaller step I'd keep.
screens.why7: The served list meets the card: the step whole in the first yes, a soft yes on a smaller step that costs no money, data or signature, two against and no escape; but the smaller-step field shows 'Yes, after a demo on sample data first' instead of the noun phrase 'a demo on sample data', and its counter says 5 words for what is shown as 8.
screens.instead: Same screen, with the smaller-step field reading just 'a demo on sample data' (5 / 9 words).

screens.why1: Right before strangers see the study is the obvious moment to decide whether to collect names for a pilot, and it follows straight from the commitment step I just set on screen 21.
screens.why2: "Offer a pilot?" with Yes/No and a one-line hint is plain to me as a founder on first read.
screens.why3: Whether I want pilot leads from this study is my own call and I know the answer: yes, I am chasing commercial GCs for pilots.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it, the two are distinct, and no escape is needed for a founder's own setting.
screens.why5: My step was "start a paid pilot on one site", but the line strangers get is a generic "Would you try this for real? Leave your email", which drops the paid and one-site parts and does not say whether supers or ops leads get it.
screens.instead: Offer your pilot at the end? Respondents see: "Would you start a paid pilot of Fresco on one of your sites? Leave your email." (Yes, ask them / No pilot)

screens.why1: Choosing the interviewer voice right before the study goes out to supers is the obvious place for it, after the pilot offer and before people see it.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but the hint packs in credits, recording once, and text links in one breath, and "face" versus "voice" leaves me unsure whether I'm picking a video face or just a voice.
screens.why3: It's my own study and my own budget, so I can answer it from what I know.
screens.why4: Two voices, each with a 5-second sample, and a default already picked is a complete and distinct choice, with no escape needed since the default covers "don't care".
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or my roles is changed here, and the respondent sees only a neutral interviewer, so nothing about Fresco leaks to them.
screens.instead: Who should ask your questions on video? Daphne is picked; tap to hear Saskia and switch (400 credits either way) -- Daphne / Saskia

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the superintendents, it makes sense to choose how the second group, the general contractor's buyers, will answer their part of the study.
screens.why2: The three choices are short and plain, and an AI interviewer that asks aloud versus reading and tapping is clear to me on first read.
screens.why3: I know my buyers are ops people at GCs who would sit at a desk with a link, so I can pick a format for them from what I know.
screens.why4: Daphne, text only, and let them pick are complete and distinct, and Read and tap, the one I picked, is there.
screens.why5: I named the buyer the contractor operations lead, and the bare word 'contractors' drifts a little, since on a jobsite it can just as well mean the subs.
screens.instead: How should the contractor operations leads answer? (AI interviewer · Daphne / Read and tap / Let them choose)

screens.why1: Once the questions are set and the interviews are sent, choosing who gets a link is the obvious last step.
screens.why2: Plain words a founder reads at first glance: people I know, people found on a search, or one open link posted to a group.
screens.why3: I know who I'd send this to, the supers and GC ops leads I've walked sites with around SF, Napa and South Bay.
screens.why4: The three ways are distinct and cover how I'd reach people, but the screen came right after 'How should contractors answer?' and doesn't say whether this choice covers the supers, the contractors, or both.
screens.why5: Nothing of Fresco or its roles is changed or leaked; it's a plain choice of how to send links.
screens.instead: Who gets a link, for supers and for contractor ops leads? People I know by name / People I found with Keel / One open link posted where they already are (each with its own pick per group).

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' is stated, and the deciding number 'Price: 1 of 8 at $800 or more per site a month' sits right beside it, though it is odd that Price is called 'not holding up' while two other cards read 'did not hold'.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart, and the strip lines take a second look: the kicker '1 TO 8 COUNTED' is cryptic, Existing sacrifice counts over 7 while the rest count over 8, and the Price card alone omits how many short of the bar it is.
screens.why_b3: Every belief is the one I set: 30 to 60 hours a month per site, $800 to $1,000 per site a month, the CFO and the project executive, a Procore check within 2 weeks, and a paid pilot on one site.
screens.why_b4: The line under the verdict only explains who was asked, and nothing tells me what to do, such as lowering the price, pricing against the 40 hours a month my supers lose, or offering a free pilot instead of a paid one.
screens.why_b5: n=8 is visible throughout, Ability to pay is honestly 'too few to call', and the one belief that holds at the bar (5 of 7) is not called strong.
screens.instead: Price fails: only 1 of 8 ops leads would pay $800 or more a site (6 needed), yet their supers lose a median 40 hours a month on the log, about $2,200 at $55 an hour. So sell against that hour cost or cut the price, and since 5 of 8 won't start a paid pilot, offer a free first site.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, 5 of 7 at 30 hours or more against a bar of 5 of 7, and the screen says it is exactly at the bar.
screens.why_b2: The strip says what it counts (hours of the daily log per site a month), over how many (7 counted, one cell each) and where the bar sits (5 of 7, at least 2 in 3) on first look.
screens.why_b3: The dimension's name and my 30-to-60-hours-per-site-a-month figure are mine, but the belief line drops 'on commercial jobs' from the people I named, so it is reworded but recognisable.
screens.why_b4: The So line only points me to the Price card I have already read (1 of 8 at $800 or more), and never says what it means that a cost of about 40 hours a month sits above my price while buyers won't pay it.
screens.why_b5: The count line says this is a small group and a lean, but the So line's flat 'The cost is there' overstates a result that sits exactly at the bar with 7 people, and Trevor's 10.9 hours is shown without saying it was converted from a dollar amount.
screens.instead: Just at the bar, 5 of 7 (a lean): most firms put about 40 hours per site a month into the log, which costs more than your $1k, yet Price fails, so test whether they count supers' hours as a real cost before cutting the price.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right beside the deciding number, 1 of 8 at $800 or more against a bar of 6 of 8.
screens.why_b2: Each band shows its count and its for or against, my $800 to $1,000 is marked on its band, and the strip shows 1 for, 7 against and the bar at 6 of 8, so it reads at once.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Price and the belief keeps my words, Fresco and my whole $800 to $1,000 per site a month range, unchanged.
screens.why_b4: The So line says 'fewer than 2 in 3', which understates a 1 of 8 result, then sends me to Insights instead of naming what the quotes on this card point to: a free one-job pilot, pricing per active super, and buyers who can't see the hours the logs cost them.
screens.why_b5: n=8 stays visible, all eight are counted, the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and nothing claims more than the answers carry.
screens.instead: Only 1 of 8 would pay $800 or more per site a month, and 5 of 8 chose under $500, so this price does not hold yet; they asked for a free first job, pricing per super using it, and proof of the hours saved, which the Existing sacrifice card puts above your price.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '1 of 8 named your price or more · 5 needed', so I know nothing is settled and why.
screens.why_b2: The chart plainly counts where the money would come from for one person (Gordon, a new line), but the strip shows a bar at 4 of 5 with four ghost cells when only 1 was asked, and the rule line leaves out 'Charged to the teams or sites that use it' even though the chart marks it for, so I had to look twice.
screens.why_b3: My price band and my buyer are there, but this belief was derived by Keel and never shown to me on the way in, and the card still calls it 'Your belief'; the rule line's 'or none' is not one of the options and 'a grant' is missing from against.
screens.why_b4: 'Ability to pay waits until 5 have' is a generic line: it doesn't say that this hangs on Price, where 1 of 8 reached $800, so no follow-up on this card will move it until the price or the buyer changes.
screens.why_b5: The count line calls one answer 'a lean, not a call', which clashes with 'Too few to call', and the So line's 'said where the money would come from' glosses over the fact that the only answer, a new budget line, counts against.
screens.instead: Too few to call: only Gordon named $800 or more, and he'd need a new budget line signed off, which counts against; this can't be read until Price holds, so fix the price or find buyers who'd pay it first.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside the number that decides it, 6 of 8 against a bar of 6 of 8, at the bar.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over 8 people, each marked for or against, and the strip shows the marker sitting on the bar at 6.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Buyer and payer and the belief line is mine: the operations lead decides, and the CFO and the project executive must agree first.
screens.why_b4: Planning for the CFO in deals while noting that 2 of 8 could sign alone is a concrete step for how I sell a site pilot.
screens.why_b5: The count line says this is a small group and a lean, not a call, but the So line's 'most deals' stretches 4 of 8 naming the CFO into most.
screens.instead: Plan for the CFO in about half your deals; 2 of 8 could sign alone, and 2 of 8 needed several people or were not the ones deciding.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside 5 of 8 under 2 weeks or not needed, bar 6 of 8, 1 short, so I see both the verdict and the number that decided it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts my 8 operations leads by band, my bar is marked at 6, and it says outright that my 2 weeks is the low edge of the 2 weeks to 1 month band, which is why that band counts against me.
screens.why_b3: It is my Procore check, my 2 weeks and my buyer, the contractor operations lead, under the Purchase friction name, close enough to how I typed it that I recognise it straight away.
screens.why_b4: "Plan for a cycle of that length" gives me a duration but not an action for the idea, such as having the Procore push working and documented before the first call, and the reason is sent off to the Insights tab.
screens.why_b5: n is shown as 8 of 8 counted and the screen says plainly that this is a small group, a lean and not a call, so nothing claims more than eight people can carry.
screens.instead: Did not hold, 1 short of 6 of 8: three of your eight, including Lena Brandt and Bill Ostrowski, expect the Procore check to take 2 weeks to a month, so walk in with the Procore push already working, or quote a month for it.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside "3 of 8 said yes · bar 6 of 8 · 3 short", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: Each of the four answers carries its count over 8 people, and the strip shows 3 for, 5 against with the marker at 6, so what is counted, over how many and where the bar sits read at once.
screens.why_b3: The card is named Commitment and the belief is mine: the contractor operations lead, start a paid pilot on one site.
screens.why_b4: The So line repeats the count and sends me to Insights; it never says that nobody took the free demo, so the problem is a hard no rather than a missing first step.
screens.why_b5: Everyone who answered is shown, the low n is flagged as "a lean, not a call", and 3 of 8 against a bar of 6 is a gap the small group can carry.
screens.instead: Only 3 of 8 ops leads would start a paid pilot on one site, and none took the free demo, so a softer first step won't close the gap; the 5 who said no or probably not are pushing back on paying at all, so look at price and who carries the cost before the pilot offer.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its status word with the deciding count beside it (1 of 8 at $800 or more against a bar of 6 of 8; 5 of 8 under 2 weeks, 1 short; 3 of 8 said yes, 3 short), so I know what failed and by how much.
screens.why_b3: The Price, Purchase friction and Commitment beliefs are the ones I checked: $800 to $1,000 per site a month, the Procore check within about 2 weeks, and a paid pilot on one site.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what these failures mean for Fresco; I have to infer my next step (a free first job, or a price not charged per site) from the quotes myself, and the two empty boxes give no hint at all.
screens.why_b5: The counts add up (2+2+3 = 7 against, and the never-saw and asked-on-Price splits account for the rest), each quote carries its pick, and nothing claims more than eight buyers can carry, though 'never saw it' beside Bill, who is quoted on Price, takes a second read.
screens.why_b6: The quotes teach me what I did not type: buyers want a free month on one job before paying, a per-site fee across many jobs pushes them toward per-supe pricing (the opposite of my 'unlimited users' pitch), signing a legal record an AI wrote is the CFO's liability worry, and one firm puts its cost at about $600 a month in overtime.
screens.instead: Price fails because buyers want to see it free on one job first and balk at a per-site fee across all jobs: test a free first month and per-supe pricing; and say why the Purchase friction and Commitment boxes have no quotes and whom to ask next.

screens.why1: This is the buying-decision link, so opening with the idea I'm being asked to price and sign off on makes sense, and the kicker tells me that's what it is.
screens.why2: Site walk, superintendents, assignees, Procore and ACC are all words I use every week, and 'AI scribe' is clear enough once it says it turns videos into notes.
screens.why3: I buy and roll out the field tools my supers use, so I can picture this on our jobs and judge it.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: The card says 'your superintendents' take the videos, but then the belief says it's 'what you use during the site walk'; I don't walk the jobs, my supers do, so the belief has slid from them to me.
screens.why6: Short, plain sentences, no slashes or brackets, and 'Procore or ACC' says fine aloud to anyone in this trade; it's a little long but easy to follow once.
screens.instead: Keep the card, but end with: The people building it believe your superintendents would use it during the site walk.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, asking what the daily log already costs us is the obvious next thing before any talk of price.
screens.why2: Daily log, site and hours are everyday words in my trade, so I get it on the first read.
screens.why3: I pay for the tools but don't watch my supers' hours on the log job by job, so I'd be estimating from what they tell me rather than recalling a number.
screens.why4: A box for a range of hours, None for zero, and I can't recall as the single escape covers every true answer without overlap.
screens.why5: It asks the founder's hours per site a month on the daily log in plain terms, and nothing of the product or its own names for people leaks through.
screens.why6: Short and one question; the 'a number of hours per site last month' tag is a little stiff but easy to hold, and the one escape is said last.
screens.why7: The box is in the founder's unit, base and period (hours per site a month), so any answer can sit above or below 30; None counts as 0 while served, and I can't recall is the one escape.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the hours-per-site question, asking what Fresco is worth per site a month is the obvious next thing to ask the person who pays.
screens.why2: Per site, per month is exactly how I think about job-site software costs, and the dollar bands read plainly.
screens.why3: I sign off on per-site tools every month, so I can answer this from what I already pay and what the daily log costs my supers.
screens.why4: The bands are complete and don't overlap, I wouldn't pay for this covers a flat no, and I can't say is the right escape.
screens.why5: Only the idea card's name and description reach me, with no founder price, plan or internal terms leaking through.
screens.why6: Four short options, then a two-way follow-up, is easy to hold by ear, and the dollar amounts say cleanly.
screens.why7: One measure in dollars per site a month, six rungs with an edge exactly at $800, two bands plus wouldn't-pay against and three bands for, and the single I can't say escape set apart.

screens.why1: Right after I put a number on it, asking what would push that number up is the obvious next thing to ask the person who pays for it.
screens.why2: It hands my answer back the way I'd say it, about $500 to $800 a site a month, and the question is plain.
screens.why3: I know what would make a daily-log tool worth more to me, like syncing straight into Procore or ACC or covering more of our sites, because I'm the one weighing what we pay for it.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: It uses only the name from the idea card and my own price, with nothing of the founder's plan or terms leaking through.
screens.why6: Two short sentences, one question, and the dollar range says easily out loud.

screens.why1: Right after I named my price, asking whether I could approve that spend myself or need the CFO is the obvious next question for the person who buys software for our job sites.
screens.why2: Sign off and CFO are everyday words in my job, and the question reads in one pass.
screens.why3: I know our approval limits and when software spend goes up to the CFO, so I'd answer from fact rather than guess, though the total across all our sites is what decides it.
screens.why4: The four run cleanly from me alone, to the CFO, to several people, to someone else's call, and I can't say covers the rest, so nothing is missing or overlapping.
screens.why5: It names my price and a role my company actually has, and nothing of the founder's product or pitch leaks in beyond the idea I was already shown.
screens.why6: It is one short either-or question with four short options said as a list and a single escape at the end, which is easy to hold by ear.
screens.why7: All four options sit on the one measure of who has to agree, in the card's order with the CFO named second, and I can't say sits apart, so the belief can be both supported and refuted.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I could sign off myself, asking what else stands between me and buying it is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: A check that it works with Procore is exactly how I would put it, since every tool on our jobs has to talk to Procore before I let a super near it.
screens.why3: I run these integration checks myself with our Procore admin, so I know roughly how long one takes for a new app.
screens.why4: The bands cover everything from a few days to a quarter-plus without gaps, and It wouldn't be needed is a real answer if it is already on the Procore marketplace; I can't tell fits as the escape.
screens.why5: Only the product's name reaches me, and the step is in my words, not a pitch.
screens.why6: The question is short, the first step is four options I can hold, and the second step's two bands say cleanly.
screens.why7: Every option is how long the step would take, the edge sits at 2 weeks with two bands and not needed for and three against, the step is a brake on my side, and I can't tell is the one escape.

screens.why1: After price, who signs off, and the Procore check, asking whether I'd actually start a pilot is the obvious last question before I'd spend anything.
screens.why2: A paid pilot on one site and a demo first are exactly how we try any new jobsite software, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: I'm the one who decides whether a tool gets piloted on one of our jobs and pays for it, so this is my call to make.
screens.why4: There's a firm yes, a cautious yes that names what I'd want first, a probably not and a no, which covers where I'd honestly land without overlap.
screens.why5: It's the founder's step word for word, and nothing in it reads like their internal plan or their terms for people beyond the idea card shown on purpose.
screens.why6: One short question and four short options I can hold after hearing them once.
screens.why7: The first option is the paid pilot as asked, the soft yes is a free smaller step that takes no money, data or signature, there are two options on each side, and there's no escape with No as the floor, so the belief can hold or fail.
